title: Chapter 9 — That The Americans Apply The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood To Religious Matters
paragraphs: If the principle of self-interest properly understood had only the present world in view, it would be very inadequate. There are many sacrifices that can find their reward only in another world. And however much ingenuity is spent on demonstrating the usefulness of virtue, it will never be easy to make a man live rightly if he gives no thought to dying. It is therefore necessary to find out whether the principle of self-interest properly understood is easily compatible with religious belief. The philosophers who teach this system of morals tell men that, to be happy in this life, they must watch their own passions and steadily control their excess. They say that lasting happiness can be secured only by giving up a thousand passing pleasures, and that a man must triumph over himself continually in order to secure his own advantage. The founders of almost all religions have said the same. The path they point out to man is the same, except that the goal is more remote. Instead of placing the reward for the sacrifices they impose in this world, they move it to another. Nevertheless, I cannot believe that all who practice virtue from religious motives are driven only by the hope of a reward. I have known zealous Christians who constantly forgot themselves in order to work with greater ardor for the happiness of their fellow men, and I have heard them declare that all they did was only to earn the blessings of a future state. I cannot help thinking that they deceive themselves. I respect them too much to believe them.

Christianity does teach that a man must prefer his neighbor to himself in order to gain eternal life. But Christianity also teaches that men ought to benefit their fellow creatures for the love of God. A sublime expression! Man searches with his intellect into the divine conception and sees that order is the purpose of God. He freely joins in carrying out the great design, and while he sacrifices his personal interests to this consummate order of all created things, he expects no other reward than the pleasure of contemplating it. I do not believe that interest is the sole motive of religious men. But I believe that interest is the principal means that religions themselves use to govern men, and I do not doubt that this is how they reach the multitude and become popular. It is not easy to see clearly why the principle of self-interest properly understood should keep away from religious opinions. It seems to me easier to show why it should draw men to them. Suppose that, in order to gain happiness in this world, a man fights his instincts on every occasion and deliberately calculates every action of his life. Suppose that, instead of yielding blindly to the force of his first desires, he has learned the art of resisting them, and has accustomed himself to sacrifice the pleasure of a moment, without effort, to the lasting interest of his whole life. If such a man believes in the religion he professes, it will cost him little to submit to the restrictions it may impose. Reason itself counsels him to obey, and habit has prepared him to endure them. If he has come to have any doubts about the object of his hopes, he will still not easily let them stop him. He will decide that it is wise to risk some of the advantages of this world in order to keep his claim to the great inheritance promised him in another. “To be mistaken in believing that the Christian religion is true,” says Pascal, “is no great loss to anyone; but how dreadful to be mistaken in believing it to be false!”

The Americans do not affect a brutal indifference to a future state. They affect no childish pride in despising perils that they hope to escape. They therefore profess their religion without shame and without weakness. But there is generally, even in their zeal, something so indescribably calm, methodical, and deliberate that it seems as if the head, far more than the heart, brought them to the foot of the altar. The Americans not only follow their religion from interest, but they often place in this world the interest that makes them follow it. In the Middle Ages the clergy spoke of nothing but a future state. They hardly cared to prove that a sincere Christian may be a happy man here below. American preachers, however, are constantly referring to the earth, and it is only with great difficulty that they can turn their attention away from it. To move their congregations, they always show how favorable religious opinions are to freedom and public tranquility. And it is often difficult to tell from their sermons whether the principal object of religion is to win eternal happiness in the other world or prosperity in this one.
